To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the structure of V. cholerae Fur reveals insights into metal coordination and that V. cholera Fur can be activated to bind DNA by a range of metals.

the V. cholaerae Fur crystal structure reveals a different orientation of the two DNA‐binding domains, compared with the P.  aeruginosa Fur crystal structure, which is the first structure of a Fur protein from a pathogenic Vibrio species.

the structure of the Vibio cholerae Fur protein reveals a different orientation of the N‐terminal DNA‐binding domains to those observed in the Pseudomonas Fur protein; the metal binding properties of the Vibrio Fur protein are different to those of the Escherichia Fur protein and that the metal binding site is different to that observed in P. aerinoginosa.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the molecular mechanism of the metal‐dependent regulation of Fur.
the structural and functional characterization of the ferric uptake regulator protein (Fur).
the molecular basis of the activation of the Fur protein, a key regulatory protein in the control of iron homeostasis and virulence in many pathogenic bacteria.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the V. cholaerae Fur structure is the first structure of a Fur protein with a metal‐binding site in each monomer and with the metal‐binding site of the regulatory domain in the correct position to be able to activate the gene‐regulating activity of the protein.
V. Cholerae Fur is a dimeric DNA‐binding protein with two metal‐binding sites per monomer.
Fur is an Fe2+‐activated repressor and that the Fe2+‐binding site is the same as the Zn2 site in the V. cholerae Fur crystal structure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
V. Cholerae Fur is a dimer with two metal binding sites per monomer.
the V. cholerae Fur structure reveals a new orientation of the DNA binding domain and that the Zn1 site is not required for DNA‐binding.
the V. chloerae Fur protein contains two distinct metal binding sites that can both be occupied by zinc.
The main takeaway from our work is that
V.  cholerae Fur is a metalloprotein that is capable of being activated by a range metals.
V. Cholerae Fur has a very different structure from that of other Fur homologues.
the metal binding properties of Fur are more diverse than previously thought.
